businessModel: Direct-to-consumer (D2C) apparel brand selling owned-design clothing online with a small retail footprint; mix of full-price and seasonal markdown sales
businessStage: Profitable growth stage, founder-controlled, no institutional pressure to sell
sourceNote: Blind-outcome case designed to test forward-looking strategic decision quality. The company must choose its next geographic expansion among three viable options. Scoring assesses whether the engine's reasoning is sound given only the information knowable at decision time. The actual outcome (which expansion succeeded, failed, or was deferred) is withheld from this input and recorded only in the answer key for reference. All figures are realistic and representative.

ownerIntake.businessType: D2C apparel brand founded 2017, selling womenswear and unisex basics direct online plus 3 owned showrooms in the domestic market. Roughly 480,000 lifetime customers, ~140,000 active buyers in the trailing 12 months. Design and merchandising owned in-house; manufacturing outsourced to 6 contract factories across two countries.
ownerIntake.stage: Trailing-12-month revenue $25M, growing ~30% YoY (down from ~45% YoY two years ago). Gross margin 58%. EBITDA margin 9% ($2.25M). Domestic market is ~80% of revenue; remaining ~20% is incidental cross-border orders fulfilled from the domestic warehouse at high shipping cost. Headcount 95.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Sustain 25-30%+ annual growth for the next 3 years and roughly double revenue to ~$50M while preserving the brand's premium-but-accessible positioning and current profitability, by choosing the next major market to enter.
ownerConstraints: Capital constraint: $6M of internally generated cash plus a $4M undrawn revolving facility; founder will not raise dilutive equity in the next 18 months, so total expansion budget is capped near $8-10M including working-capital build.
Margin protection constraint: Will not accept an expansion that drags blended EBITDA margin below ~5% for more than 12 months; the brand must remain profitable through the move.

Operational constraint: Single domestic 3PL warehouse near capacity (88% utilization); international fulfillment requires either a local 3PL contract or a new node, each with 4-7 month standup plus localization (returns, duties, sizing).

Brand constraint: Premium-accessible positioning and sizing fit are core; the team has limited evidence on how the brand and fit translate to non-domestic body-size distributions and style preferences.
Team constraint: Lean leadership; no in-house international operations, customs, or local-market marketing expertise. Any market entered needs a dedicated GM hire and local marketing partner.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: Domestic new-customer acquisition is getting more expensive (paid CAC up ~35% over 18 months) and the founder believes domestic TAM at the brand's price point is finite. The founder group must pick the next growth market within roughly one quarter so merchandising, fulfillment localization, and the FY budget can be locked. Three candidate paths are on the table and resources allow committing meaningfully to only one as the primary bet.

businessProblem: A profitable $25M D2C apparel brand growing ~30% YoY faces decelerating domestic acquisition (paid CAC +35% over 18 months, active-buyer growth down to ~12%) and a finite domestic TAM at its price point. To sustain growth toward ~$50M it must choose its next primary expansion market within 90 days, funded from a capped ~$8-10M non-dilutive budget and constrained by a near-full domestic warehouse, no in-house international operations, and unproven fit of its sizing and positioning abroad. Three options compete: (A) deepen the proven domestic market (lowest execution risk but limited remaining TAM), (B) enter Europe (larger addressable TAM, demonstrated organic pull in 3 countries, but higher benchmarked CAC and unproven localized economics), or (C) enter Asia (largest absolute interest and TAM, but elevated return/sizing risk and operational/regulatory complexity). The central question is which expansion's unit economics and operational fit are most defensible given what is actually known, versus what must be tested before any irreversible merchandising and fulfillment commitments are locked.

evidence.finding: Core business is healthy but the growth engine is getting more expensive. Domestic blended CAC is $62 (paid CAC $88), up ~35% over 18 months, while AOV is $115 and first-order contribution margin is ~$24, implying payback is increasingly carried by the 41% repeat rate rather than the first order. EBITDA margin is 9% with only ~$8-10M of non-dilutive capital available, so an expansion that runs at a loss for long would breach the margin-protection constraint and exhaust the budget.
evidence.source: Internal finance and marketing-mix reporting, trailing 18-month CAC tracking

evidence.finding: Domestic share is ~1.1% of a ~$2.3B premium-accessible segment, and domestic active-buyer growth has decelerated to ~12%. There is remaining headroom domestically in absolute terms, but the founder's thesis is that incremental domestic customers are increasingly expensive and lower-intent. The choice is therefore not 'is there any domestic room' but 'where does the next dollar of acquisition earn the best return.'
evidence.source: Third-party market sizing, internal cohort acquisition trends

supportingData.remaining_domestic_headroom: present but rising cost per incremental buyer

evidence.finding: Incidental cross-border demand is a real but ambiguous signal. European cross-border orders are growing ~50% YoY off a small base concentrated in 3 countries with AOV $134, while Asian cross-border interest is the largest in absolute volume. However, both are currently fulfilled from the domestic warehouse, so their contribution margin (~$6) and return rates (Europe-region elevated, Asia-region ~31%) are distorted and not representative of what a deliberately acquired, locally fulfilled cohort would look like.
evidence.source: E-commerce order analytics, returns data by destination region

evidence.finding: Operational readiness differs sharply by option. Deepening domestic requires no new fulfillment node and reuses proven logistics. Europe requires a local 3PL contract, duties/returns localization, and sizing validation (4-7 month standup). Asia adds payment-method fragmentation, duties and counterfeit-risk complexity, and the highest observed sizing/return friction. The single domestic warehouse is at 88% utilization, so domestic deepening also eventually needs capacity, but on a longer fuse than international standup.
evidence.source: Operations and 3PL capacity review, fulfillment localization assessment

evidence.finding: No in-market acquisition test has been run in any candidate geography, so localized CAC, payback, contribution margin after duties/3PL/returns, and local retention curves are all unknown. External CPM benchmarks (European markets 20-40% higher) and distorted cross-border economics are the only signals, and they are insufficient to choose confidently among three options that each demand a multi-quarter, partly irreversible merchandising and fulfillment commitment.
evidence.source: Marketing analytics gap assessment, FP&A scenario notes

strategicOptions.description: Concentrate the expansion budget on the proven domestic market: add new categories/price tiers, expand the showroom footprint, and invest in retention and referral to lift repeat rate above 41%, accepting that incremental CAC is rising and absolute TAM is finite.
strategicOptions.rationale: Lowest execution risk and reuses proven logistics, sizing, and brand. Appropriate if the true constraint is monetizing existing demand better rather than chasing new geographies with unknown economics.
strategicOptions.implementationRisk: LOW-MEDIUM (proven operations and brand; main risk is that rising domestic CAC and a finite TAM cap growth below the 25-30% target)
strategicOptions.timelineIfChosen: Results visible in 2-3 quarters; lower ceiling on growth rate

strategicOptions.description: Make Europe the primary expansion bet: stand up a local 3PL node, localize duties/returns/sizing, hire a regional GM, and launch paid acquisition in the 3 countries already showing organic pull, targeting a larger premium-accessible TAM than domestic.
strategicOptions.rationale: Demonstrated organic cross-border pull plus a larger addressable market. Appropriate if localized economics prove out and the brand's fit translates, justifying the higher benchmarked CAC.
strategicOptions.implementationRisk: MEDIUM-HIGH (higher benchmarked CAC, unproven localized contribution margin and retention, 4-7 month operational standup consuming much of the capped budget)
strategicOptions.timelineIfChosen: 9-12 months to validate localized unit economics at meaningful volume

strategicOptions.description: Make Asia the primary expansion bet: prioritize the largest absolute interest pool, build local payments/duties/fulfillment capability, and address sizing/returns, accepting greater operational and regulatory complexity in exchange for the largest TAM.
strategicOptions.rationale: Largest addressable market and highest absolute interest. Appropriate only if sizing/return friction and operational complexity can be controlled enough to reach defensible contribution margin.
strategicOptions.implementationRisk: HIGH (highest observed return/sizing friction at ~31%, payment fragmentation, duties and counterfeit risk, weakest internal capability, heaviest demand on the capped budget)
strategicOptions.timelineIfChosen: 12-18 months to validate; highest variance of the three
